Threat.value: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns

issues.explanation: For an 18-year-old male whose trauma type is rape, the trigger 'Military Topics' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The other trigger, threat, and memory items coherently suggest interpersonal/close-contact danger (touch, strangers, shouting, doors, vivid sensory reliving), but military-related talk implies a trauma context that is otherwise absent. This is not supported by the threat or memory content and does not fit the formulation as a plausible trigger tightly linked to the presented threat-memory pattern.

vignette:
Amari was eighteen years old and had been working as a tax consultant for just under a year when the attack happened. He had joined a mid-sized firm after completing a fast-track certification program, the youngest in his department. It was a late evening in February, and he was still at his desk, finishing a quarterly reconciliation for a client. A senior colleague-a man Amari had trusted and looked up to-asked him to stay behind to review a file together. Amari agreed. He remembered the sound of the office door clicking shut, the way the senior colleague's tone shifted from professional to something sharper, and then the shouting. Amari could not recall the exact words, only the volume and the fact that it happened in a room where no one else was around. That did not matter. The colleague's weight, the hands on his body, the taste of his own tears mixing with something metallic in his mouth-Amari would never forget any of it.

In the weeks that followed, the world became a place of hidden dangers. Amari found himself scanning every room before he entered, trying to calculate how many men were inside, whether he could see all the exits. He began to avoid unfamiliar places entirely: new restaurants, friends' apartments, even a different branch of his own office. If he could not assess the danger beforehand, he stayed home. The startle response came first, then the avoidance. When a colleague touched his shoulder unexpectedly one morning, Amari flinched so violently that he knocked his coffee cup off the desk. He started to walk through the office with his shoulders hunched, his hands in his pockets, hoping no one would reach for him.

The memories came in two forms. Sometimes they appeared as vivid, snapshot images: the pattern on the office carpet, the senior colleague's tie, the angle of the desk lamp. Other times, Amari would be standing in line at the grocery store and suddenly feel the full weight of the terror-the helplessness, the nausea-without any picture in his mind. He would find himself sweating, his heart pounding, for no reason he could name. And then there was the taste. Every now and then, without warning, the metallic, salty taste would flood his mouth, and he knew it was the same taste he had experienced that night. It made him gag.

At work, Amari avoided being alone with any man. He would wait for another person to be in the conference room before entering. He stopped staying late. When a male manager asked him to step into his office, Amari would say he had a deadline and could talk in the open workspace instead. The avoidance worked in the moment, but it also drew attention. His supervisor noticed he was not taking new client meetings unless a female colleague was present. Amari could not explain why. He just knew that the sight of a door closing behind him with a man inside made his chest tighten, and the sound of a door slamming anywhere in the building made him jump so badly that he had to excuse himself to the restroom.

Shouting was the worst trigger. One afternoon, a heated argument broke out between two colleagues in the next cubicle. Amari froze at his desk, his hands gripping the armrests, his vision narrowing. He could hear the shouting but not the words-all he could feel was the same trapped panic. He left the office early that day and did not come back for three days, telling himself he was sick. He had come to believe that any unfamiliar man approaching him might be a threat, and that the only way to be safe was to stay in places he already knew, with people he already trusted.

The cumulative cost was growing. Amari had stopped seeing his friends. He worked from home when he could, but his performance slipped. His relationships with family members became strained; his mother asked why he flinched when she touched him. He knew he could not keep living this way. What finally brought him into a clinician's office was a panic attack that lasted an hour after a delivery man shouted an apology through his apartment door. Amari wanted the memories to stop, but more than that, he wanted to walk into an unfamiliar building without feeling like he was about to die. He was terrified that the therapy itself would force him to talk about what happened, but he was also desperate enough to try.
